\section{How to read this document}
\noindent Each theorem is printed as Lean source, not re-typeset in mathematical notation, so that the statement the kernel checked and the statement on the page cannot differ. A proof by \texttt{decide} reduces a finite proposition in the kernel and depends on no axiom. A general theorem, proved for every value, rests on \texttt{propext} and \texttt{Quot.sound} and on nothing else; the gate refuses any theorem that reaches \texttt{Classical.choice}. To re-check everything from a clone, run \texttt{npm run verify:lean}.

\subsection{\texttt{coin.lean}}
\begin{theorem}[The coin is an involution]
PULLED, AND REFLECTED BACK. Applying the map twice returns the origin, for every digit: the black-hole side and the white-hole side are two orbits of ONE map, not two mechanisms.
\begin{lean}∀ d ∈ digits, σ (σ d) = d\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{coin.lean}:\begin{lean}def σ (\allowbreak{}d : Nat) : Nat := 1\allowbreak{}0 - d\\
\mbox{}\\
def digits : List Nat := [\allowbreak{}1,\allowbreak{} 2,\allowbreak{} 3,\allowbreak{} 4,\allowbreak{} 5,\allowbreak{} 6,\allowbreak{} 7,\allowbreak{} 8,\allowbreak{} 9]\end{lean}
The proof, verbatim as the Lean kernel checked it:\begin{lean}theorem the\_\allowbreak{}coin\_\allowbreak{}is\_\allowbreak{}an\_\allowbreak{}involution : ∀ d ∈ digits,\allowbreak{} σ (\allowbreak{}σ d) = d := by decide\end{lean}
It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{of\_decide\_eq\_true} (the kernel itself: the statement reduces to true by computation, and the rule that turns that reduction into a proof rests on no axiom). \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[The harmonic is the only fixed point]
HARMONIC IS WHAT THE MAP LEAVES IN PLACE, and there is exactly one such digit. The fixed point is not chosen; it is computed by filtering the surface.
\begin{lean}digits.filter (fun d => σ d == d) = [5]\end{lean}
\end{theorem}

It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{of\_decide\_eq\_true} (the kernel itself: the statement reduces to true by computation, and the rule that turns that reduction into a proof rests on no axiom). \end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The sides are equal and exchanged]
The first form of this said `∀ d ∈ below, σ d ∈ above` — membership as the PREDICATE — and the kernel reported it dependent on propext and Quot.sound. The axiom-freedom gate refused it, and the restatement is stronger for it: naming the image list says WHICH element goes where, not merely that each lands somewhere on the other side.
\begin{lean}below.length = above.length ∧ below.map σ = above.reverse ∧ above.map σ = below.reverse\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{coin.lean}:\begin{lean}def σ (\allowbreak{}d : Nat) : Nat := 1\allowbreak{}0 - d\\
\mbox{}\\

\mbox{}\\

The proof, verbatim as the Lean kernel checked it:\begin{lean}theorem the\_\allowbreak{}sides\_\allowbreak{}are\_\allowbreak{}equal\_\allowbreak{}and\_\allowbreak{}exchanged : below.\allowbreak{}length = above.\allowbreak{}length ∧ below.\allowbreak{}map σ = above.\allowbreak{}reverse ∧ above.\allowbreak{}map σ = below.\allowbreak{}reverse := by decide\end{lean}

\begin{theorem}[The coin is two sides and one edge]
The surface is exactly the two sides and the edge, and σ itself sorts it: the digits it carries upward are `below`, the one it leaves in place is the edge, the digits it carries downward are `above` — so the sides are computed from the map rather than typed beside it, and 4 + 4 + 1 is what the sorting leaves. (Was the count alone, which read the two typed lists back, 2026-09-14.)
\begin{lean}digits.filter (fun d => d < σ d) = below ∧ digits.filter (fun d => σ d == d) = [5] ∧ digits.filter (fun d => σ d < d) = above ∧ below.length + above.length + 1 = digits.length\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{coin.lean}:\begin{lean}def σ (\allowbreak{}d : Nat) : Nat := 1\allowbreak{}0 - d\\
\mbox{}\\
def digits : List Nat := [\allowbreak{}1,\allowbreak{} 2,\allowbreak{} 3,\allowbreak{} 4,\allowbreak{} 5,\allowbreak{} 6,\allowbreak{} 7,\allowbreak{} 8,\allowbreak{} 9]\\
\mbox{}\\
def below : List Nat := [\allowbreak{}1,\allowbreak{} 2,\allowbreak{} 3,\allowbreak{} 4]\\
\mbox{}\\
def above : List Nat := [\allowbreak{}6,\allowbreak{} 7,\allowbreak{} 8,\allowbreak{} 9]\end{lean}
The proof, verbatim as the Lean kernel checked it:\begin{lean}theorem the\_\allowbreak{}coin\_\allowbreak{}is\_\allowbreak{}two\_\allowbreak{}sides\_\allowbreak{}and\_\allowbreak{}one\_\allowbreak{}edge : digits.\allowbreak{}filter (\allowbreak{}fun d => d < σ d) = below ∧ digits.\allowbreak{}filter (\allowbreak{}fun d => σ d == d) = [\allowbreak{}5] ∧ digits.\allowbreak{}filter (\allowbreak{}fun d => σ d < d) = above ∧ below.\allowbreak{}length + above.\allowbreak{}length + 1 = digits.\allowbreak{}length := by decide\end{lean}
It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{of\_decide\_eq\_true} (the kernel itself: the statement reduces to true by computation, and the rule that turns that reduction into a proof rests on no axiom). \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Every bit of resistance drains]
EVERY BIT OF RESISTANCE DRAINS. Resistance is ODD under the involution — r(σd) = −r(d) — so each orbit sums to exactly zero. Nothing is left over anywhere on the surface.
\begin{lean}∀ d ∈ digits, resistance d + resistance (σ d) = 0\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright

\mbox{}\\
def resistance (\allowbreak{}d : Nat) : Int := (\allowbreak{}d : Int) - (\allowbreak{}σ d : Int)\end{lean}

It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{of\_decide\_eq\_true} (the kernel itself: the statement reduces to true by computation, and the rule that turns that reduction into a proof rests on no axiom). \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[The harmonic carries no resistance]
The harmonic point is the one that never had any: at the fixed point the resistance is zero before any folding, which is what makes it the edge rather than a side.
\begin{lean}resistance 5 = 0\end{lean}
\end{theorem}

\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[The drain is exact at every scale]
The drain is not an approximation that improves with scale: it is exact at every multiple, because oddness is preserved by scaling. Checked at four magnitudes.
\begin{lean}∀ k ∈ [1, 10, 1000, 1000000], (digits.map (fun d => k * resistance d)).sum = 0\end{lean}
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Finite verification does not entail the universal]
So a finite verification does not entail the unbounded claim: here is a property verified at a thousand consecutive points whose universal statement is FALSE. This is the whole reason a `by decide` proof over a finite list is not a proof of a conjecture over an infinite domain.
\begin{lean}((List.range 1000).all holdsBelowAThousand = true) ∧ (holdsBelowAThousand 1000 = false)\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{decidability.lean}:\begin{lean}def holdsBelowAThousand (\allowbreak{}n : Nat) : Bool := n != 1\allowbreak{}0\allowbreak{}0\allowbreak{}0\end{lean}

by\\

\begin{theorem}[The clay files quantify over finite lists]
The corpus's Clay-named theorems quantify over finite lists of this size — nine points for the Riemann functional equation, seven for BSD. Recorded as arithmetic so the scale is not rhetorical: a nine-element check is nine cases, and the set of non-trivial zeros of ζ is not nine.

\subsection{\texttt{involution.lean}}
\begin{theorem}[Orbit sums to zero]
THE ODD PART CANCELS OVER EVERY ORBIT. For any involution, any f, any point: the pair \{x, σx\} sums to exactly zero. This is the general form of "every bit of resistance drains", and the coin's version of it is this theorem at σ d = 10 − d.
\begin{lean}\{α : Type\} (f : α → Int) (σ : α → α) (h : IsInvolution σ) (x : α) : odd f σ x + odd f σ (σ x) = 0\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{involution.lean}:\begin{lean}def IsInvolution \{α : Type\} (\allowbreak{}σ : α → α) : Prop := ∀ x,\allowbreak{} σ (\allowbreak{}σ x) = x\\
\mbox{}\\
def odd \{α : Type\} (\allowbreak{}f : α → Int) (\allowbreak{}σ : α → α) (\allowbreak{}x : α) : Int := f x - f (\allowbreak{}σ x)\\
\mbox{}\\
def σ (\allowbreak{}d : Nat) : Nat := 1\allowbreak{}0 - d\end{lean}
The proof, verbatim as the Lean kernel checked it:\begin{lean}theorem orbit\_\allowbreak{}sums\_\allowbreak{}to\_\allowbreak{}zero : \{α : Type\} (\allowbreak{}f : α → Int) (\allowbreak{}σ : α → α) (\allowbreak{}h : IsInvolution σ) (\allowbreak{}x : α) : odd f σ x + odd f σ (\allowbreak{}σ x) = 0 :=\\
by\\
\ \ unfold odd\\
\ \ rw [\allowbreak{}h x,\allowbreak{} Int.\allowbreak{}sub\_\allowbreak{}eq\_\allowbreak{}add\_\allowbreak{}neg,\allowbreak{} Int.\allowbreak{}sub\_\allowbreak{}eq\_\allowbreak{}add\_\allowbreak{}neg,\allowbreak{} Int.\allowbreak{}add\_\allowbreak{}assoc,\allowbreak{}\\
\ \ \ \ \ \ ← Int.\allowbreak{}add\_\allowbreak{}assoc (\allowbreak{}-f (\allowbreak{}σ x)),\allowbreak{} Int.\allowbreak{}add\_\allowbreak{}left\_\allowbreak{}neg,\allowbreak{} Int.\allowbreak{}zero\_\allowbreak{}add,\allowbreak{} Int.\allowbreak{}add\_\allowbreak{}right\_\allowbreak{}neg]\end{lean}
It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{propext} (two propositions that imply each other are the same proposition). \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Odd vanishes at a fixed point]
THE HARMONIC POINT CARRIES NOTHING. Wherever σ fixes a point, the odd part is zero there — no involution hypothesis is needed, only that this point is fixed.
\begin{lean}\{α : Type\} (f : α → Int) (σ : α → α) (x : α) (hx : σ x = x) : odd f σ x = 0\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{involution.lean}:\begin{lean}def odd \{α : Type\} (\allowbreak{}f : α → Int) (\allowbreak{}σ : α → α) (\allowbreak{}x : α) : Int := f x - f (\allowbreak{}σ x)\\
\mbox{}\\
def σ (\allowbreak{}d : Nat) : Nat := 1\allowbreak{}0 - d\end{lean}
The proof, verbatim as the Lean kernel checked it:\begin{lean}theorem odd\_\allowbreak{}vanishes\_\allowbreak{}at\_\allowbreak{}a\_\allowbreak{}fixed\_\allowbreak{}point : \{α : Type\} (\allowbreak{}f : α → Int) (\allowbreak{}σ : α → α) (\allowbreak{}x : α) (\allowbreak{}hx : σ x = x) : odd f σ x = 0 :=\\
by\\
\ \ unfold odd\\
\ \ rw [\allowbreak{}hx,\allowbreak{} Int.\allowbreak{}sub\_\allowbreak{}self]\end{lean}
It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{propext} (two propositions that imply each other are the same proposition). \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[EvenPart is symmetric]
THE EVEN PART IS WHAT SURVIVES THE REFLECTION — it takes the same value at x and at σx.
\begin{lean}\{α : Type\} (f : α → Int) (σ : α → α) (h : IsInvolution σ) (x : α) : evenPart f σ (σ x) = evenPart f σ x\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{involution.lean}:\begin{lean}def IsInvolution \{α : Type\} (\allowbreak{}σ : α → α) : Prop := ∀ x,\allowbreak{} σ (\allowbreak{}σ x) = x\\
\mbox{}\\
def evenPart \{α : Type\} (\allowbreak{}f : α → Int) (\allowbreak{}σ : α → α) (\allowbreak{}x : α) : Int := f x + f (\allowbreak{}σ x)\\

\begin{theorem}[Light is the fixed point]
LIGHT IS THE FIXED POINT OF COMPOSITION. Add any velocity to c and the result is c again — not approximately, not in a limit: the same fraction, exactly, at every sample. This is the sense in which c is not a speed among speeds but the fixed point of the operation that combines them.
\begin{lean}∀ v ∈ sample, same (add light v) light = true\end{lean}
\end{theorem}

\mbox{}\\
def light : Vel := ⟨\allowbreak{}1,\allowbreak{} 1⟩\\
\mbox{}\\

\mbox{}\\

\begin{theorem}[The boost preserves the interval]
THE INTERVAL IS INVARIANT UP TO THE ONE COMMON FACTOR. For every event and every boost, the boosted interval equals the original times (q² − p²) — the same factor throughout, independent of the event, which is exactly what "the boost preserves the interval" means once denominators are cleared.

\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[The reverse boost undoes the boost]
THE BOOST IS UNDONE BY THE REVERSE BOOST. \begin{theorem}[The reverse boost undoes every boost]
…and for EVERY event and EVERY boost, proved rather than decided: the theorem above checks eight events under five boosts; this holds for all integers p, q, t, x at once. Multiplying out leaves q²t − qpx + pqx − p²t, and the cross terms cancel because multiplication commutes. A proof, not an exhaustion — it rests on the standard axioms propext and Quot.sound that core's integer lemmas carry.
\begin{lean}∀ p q t x : Int, boostT (-p) q (boostT p q t x) (boostX p q t x) = (q * q - p * p) * t ∧ boostX (-p) q (boostT p q t x) (boostX p q t x) = (q * q - p * p) * x\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{spacetime.lean}:\begin{lean}def boostT (\allowbreak{}p q t x : Int) : Int := q * t - p * x\\
\mbox{}\\
def boostX (\allowbreak{}p q t x : Int) : Int := q * x - p * t\end{lean}
The proof, verbatim as the Lean kernel checked it:\begin{lean}theorem the\_\allowbreak{}reverse\_\allowbreak{}boost\_\allowbreak{}undoes\_\allowbreak{}every\_\allowbreak{}boost : ∀ p q t x : Int,\allowbreak{} boostT (\allowbreak{}-p) q (\allowbreak{}boostT p q t x) (\allowbreak{}boostX p q t x) = (\allowbreak{}q * q - p * p) * t ∧ boostX (\allowbreak{}-p) q (\allowbreak{}boostT p q t x) (\allowbreak{}boostX p q t x) = (\allowbreak{}q * q - p * p) * x :=\\
by\\
\ \ intro p q t x\\
\ \ unfold boostT boostX\\
\ \ have h1 : q * (\allowbreak{}p * x) = p * (\allowbreak{}q * x) := Int.\allowbreak{}mul\_\allowbreak{}left\_\allowbreak{}comm q p x\\
\ \ have h2 : q * (\allowbreak{}p * t) = p * (\allowbreak{}q * t) := Int.\allowbreak{}mul\_\allowbreak{}left\_\allowbreak{}comm q p t\\
\ \ have h3 : q * (\allowbreak{}q * t) = q * q * t := (\allowbreak{}Int.\allowbreak{}mul\_\allowbreak{}assoc q q t).\allowbreak{}symm\\
\ \ have h4 : p * (\allowbreak{}p * t) = p * p * t := (\allowbreak{}Int.\allowbreak{}mul\_\allowbreak{}assoc p p t).\allowbreak{}symm\\
\ \ have h5 : q * (\allowbreak{}q * x) = q * q * x := (\allowbreak{}Int.\allowbreak{}mul\_\allowbreak{}assoc q q x).\allowbreak{}symm\\
\ \ have h6 : p * (\allowbreak{}p * x) = p * p * x := (\allowbreak{}Int.\allowbreak{}mul\_\allowbreak{}assoc p p x).\allowbreak{}symm\\
\ \ simp only [\allowbreak{}Int.\allowbreak{}mul\_\allowbreak{}sub,\allowbreak{} Int.\allowbreak{}sub\_\allowbreak{}mul,\allowbreak{} Int.\allowbreak{}neg\_\allowbreak{}mul]\\
\ \ constructor <;> omega\end{lean}
It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{Quot.sound} (a quotient makes equal what its relation relates — the axiom behind function extensionality) and \texttt{propext} (two propositions that imply each other are the same proposition). \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Sq lt]
Strictly inside the band (−b, b) means a strictly smaller square.
\begin{lean}(a b : Int) (hl : -b < a) (hr : a < b) : a*a < b*b\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
The proof, verbatim as the Lean kernel checked it:\begin{lean}theorem sq\_\allowbreak{}lt : (\allowbreak{}a b : Int) (\allowbreak{}hl : -b < a) (\allowbreak{}hr : a < b) : a*a < b*b :=\\
by\\
\ \ have hp : 0 < (\allowbreak{}b - a) * (\allowbreak{}b + a) := Int.\allowbreak{}mul\_\allowbreak{}pos (\allowbreak{}by omega) (\allowbreak{}by omega)\\
\ \ expand\_\allowbreak{}omega\end{lean}
It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{Quot.sound} (a quotient makes equal what its relation relates — the axiom behind function extensionality) and \texttt{propext} (two propositions that imply each other are the same proposition). \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Lt of sq]
A smaller square (with b positive) means inside the band.
\begin{lean}(a b : Int) (hb : 0 < b) (h : a*a < b*b) : -b < a ∧ a < b\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
The proof, verbatim as the Lean kernel checked it:\begin{lean}theorem lt\_\allowbreak{}of\_\allowbreak{}sq : (\allowbreak{}a b : Int) (\allowbreak{}hb : 0 < b) (\allowbreak{}h : a*a < b*b) : -b < a ∧ a < b :=\\
by\\
\ \ refine ⟨\allowbreak{}?\_\allowbreak{},\allowbreak{} ?\_\allowbreak{}⟩\\
\ \ · by\_\allowbreak{}cases hc : -b < a\\
\ \ \ \ · exact hc\\
\ \ \ \ · have k := Int.\allowbreak{}mul\_\allowbreak{}nonneg (\allowbreak{}by omega : (\allowbreak{}0:Int) ≤ b - a) (\allowbreak{}by omega : (\allowbreak{}0:Int) ≤ -(\allowbreak{}b + a))\\
\ \ \ \ \ \ exfalso; expand\_\allowbreak{}omega\\
\ \ · by\_\allowbreak{}cases hc : a < b\\
\ \ \ \ · exact hc\\
\ \ \ \ · have k := Int.\allowbreak{}mul\_\allowbreak{}nonneg (\allowbreak{}by omega : (\allowbreak{}0:Int) ≤ -(\allowbreak{}b - a)) (\allowbreak{}by omega : (\allowbreak{}0:Int) ≤ b + a)\\
\ \ \ \ \ \ exfalso; expand\_\allowbreak{}omega\end{lean}
It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{Quot.sound} (a quotient makes equal what its relation relates — the axiom behind function extensionality) and \texttt{propext} (two propositions that imply each other are the same proposition). \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Interval scales]
For every event and every boost the interval is multiplied by q² − p², and by nothing else.
\begin{lean}(p q t x : Int) : interval (boostT p q t x) (boostX p q t x) = (q*q - p*p) * interval t x\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{spacetime.lean}:\begin{lean}def interval (\allowbreak{}t x : Int) : Int := t * t - x * x\\
\mbox{}\\
def boostT (\allowbreak{}p q t x : Int) : Int := q * t - p * x\\
\mbox{}\\
def boostX (\allowbreak{}p q t x : Int) : Int := q * x - p * t\end{lean}
The proof, verbatim as the Lean kernel checked it:\begin{lean}theorem interval\_\allowbreak{}scales : (\allowbreak{}p q t x : Int) : interval (\allowbreak{}boostT p q t x) (\allowbreak{}boostX p q t x) = (\allowbreak{}q*q - p*p) * interval t x :=\\
by\\
\ \ unfold interval boostT boostX; expand\_\allowbreak{}omega\end{lean}
It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{Quot.sound} (a quotient makes equal what its relation relates — the axiom behind function extensionality) and \texttt{propext} (two propositions that imply each other are the same proposition). \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Scale positive]
Below c that factor is positive.
\begin{lean}(p q : Int) (h : belowC p q) : 0 < q*q - p*p\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{spacetime.lean}:\begin{lean}def belowC (\allowbreak{}p q : Int) : Prop := 0 < q ∧ -q < p ∧ p < q\end{lean}
The proof, verbatim as the Lean kernel checked it:\begin{lean}theorem scale\_\allowbreak{}positive : (\allowbreak{}p q : Int) (\allowbreak{}h : belowC p q) : 0 < q*q - p*p :=\\
by\\
\ \ obtain ⟨\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{},\allowbreak{} hl,\allowbreak{} hr⟩ := h\\
\ \ have := sq\_\allowbreak{}lt p q hl hr; omega\end{lean}
It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{Quot.sound} (a quotient makes equal what its relation relates — the axiom behind function extensionality) and \texttt{propext} (two propositions that imply each other are the same proposition). \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Timelike invariant]
TIMELIKE STAYS TIMELIKE in every frame below c.
\begin{lean}(p q t x : Int) (h : belowC p q) (ht : 0 < interval t x) : 0 < interval (boostT p q t x) (boostX p q t x)\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{spacetime.lean}:\begin{lean}def interval (\allowbreak{}t x : Int) : Int := t * t - x * x\\
\mbox{}\\
def boostT (\allowbreak{}p q t x : Int) : Int := q * t - p * x\\
\mbox{}\\
def boostX (\allowbreak{}p q t x : Int) : Int := q * x - p * t\\
\mbox{}\\
def belowC (\allowbreak{}p q : Int) : Prop := 0 < q ∧ -q < p ∧ p < q\end{lean}
The proof, verbatim as the Lean kernel checked it:\begin{lean}theorem timelike\_\allowbreak{}invariant : (\allowbreak{}p q t x : Int) (\allowbreak{}h : belowC p q) (\allowbreak{}ht : 0 < interval t x) : 0 < interval (\allowbreak{}boostT p q t x) (\allowbreak{}boostX p q t x) :=\\
by\\
\ \ have hs := scale\_\allowbreak{}positive p q h\\
\ \ rw [\allowbreak{}interval\_\allowbreak{}scales]; exact Int.\allowbreak{}mul\_\allowbreak{}pos hs ht\end{lean}
It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{Quot.sound} (a quotient makes equal what its relation relates — the axiom behind function extensionality) and \texttt{propext} (two propositions that imply each other are the same proposition). \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Spacelike invariant]
SPACELIKE STAYS SPACELIKE: no boost makes a spacelike separation reachable.
\begin{lean}(p q t x : Int) (h : belowC p q) (ht : interval t x < 0) : interval (boostT p q t x) (boostX p q t x) < 0\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{spacetime.lean}:\begin{lean}def interval (\allowbreak{}t x : Int) : Int := t * t - x * x\\

def belowC (\allowbreak{}p q : Int) : Prop := 0 < q ∧ -q < p ∧ p < q\end{lean}
The proof, verbatim as the Lean kernel checked it:\begin{lean}theorem spacelike\_\allowbreak{}invariant : (\allowbreak{}p q t x : Int) (\allowbreak{}h : belowC p q) (\allowbreak{}ht : interval t x < 0) : interval (\allowbreak{}boostT p q t x) (\allowbreak{}boostX p q t x) < 0 :=\\
by\\

\begin{theorem}[Null invariant]
The light cone is frame-independent: null in one frame is null in all.
\begin{lean}(p q t x : Int) (ht : interval t x = 0) : interval (boostT p q t x) (boostX p q t x) = 0\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{spacetime.lean}:\begin{lean}def interval (\allowbreak{}t x : Int) : Int := t * t - x * x\\
\mbox{}\\
def boostT (\allowbreak{}p q t x : Int) : Int := q * t - p * x\\
\mbox{}\\
def boostX (\allowbreak{}p q t x : Int) : Int := q * x - p * t\end{lean}
The proof, verbatim as the Lean kernel checked it:\begin{lean}theorem null\_\allowbreak{}invariant : (\allowbreak{}p q t x : Int) (\allowbreak{}ht : interval t x = 0) : interval (\allowbreak{}boostT p q t x) (\allowbreak{}boostX p q t x) = 0 :=\\
by\\
\ \ rw [\allowbreak{}interval\_\allowbreak{}scales,\allowbreak{} ht]; exact Int.\allowbreak{}mul\_\allowbreak{}zero \_\allowbreak{}\end{lean}

\begin{theorem}[Timelike order absolute]
FOR A CAUSAL SEPARATION EVERY OBSERVER BELOW c AGREES WHICH EVENT CAME FIRST. The closed cone: the null case |x| = t is in, because a light signal carries causation too.
\begin{lean}(p q t x : Int) (h : belowC p q) (hfuture : 0 < t) (hcausal : x*x ≤ t*t) : 0 < boostT p q t x\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{spacetime.lean}:\begin{lean}def boostT (\allowbreak{}p q t x : Int) : Int := q * t - p * x\\
\mbox{}\\
def belowC (\allowbreak{}p q : Int) : Prop := 0 < q ∧ -q < p ∧ p < q\end{lean}
The proof, verbatim as the Lean kernel checked it:\begin{lean}theorem timelike\_\allowbreak{}order\_\allowbreak{}absolute : (\allowbreak{}p q t x : Int) (\allowbreak{}h : belowC p q) (\allowbreak{}hfuture : 0 < t) (\allowbreak{}hcausal : x*x ≤ t*t) : 0 < boostT p q t x :=\\
by\\
\ \ obtain ⟨\allowbreak{}hq,\allowbreak{} hl,\allowbreak{} hr⟩ := h\\
\ \ have hbl : -t ≤ x := by\\
\ \ \ \ by\_\allowbreak{}cases hc : -t ≤ x\\
\ \ \ \ · exact hc\\
\ \ \ \ · have k := Int.\allowbreak{}mul\_\allowbreak{}pos (\allowbreak{}by omega : (\allowbreak{}0:Int) < t - x) (\allowbreak{}by omega : (\allowbreak{}0:Int) < -(\allowbreak{}t + x))\\
\ \ \ \ \ \ exfalso; expand\_\allowbreak{}omega\\
\ \ have hbr : x ≤ t := by\\
\ \ \ \ by\_\allowbreak{}cases hc : x ≤ t\\
\ \ \ \ · exact hc\\
\ \ \ \ · have k := Int.\allowbreak{}mul\_\allowbreak{}pos (\allowbreak{}by omega : (\allowbreak{}0:Int) < -(\allowbreak{}t - x)) (\allowbreak{}by omega : (\allowbreak{}0:Int) < t + x)\\
\ \ \ \ \ \ exfalso; expand\_\allowbreak{}omega\\
\ \ -- 2(\allowbreak{}qt − px) = (\allowbreak{}q−p)(\allowbreak{}t+x) + (\allowbreak{}q+p)(\allowbreak{}t−x): both terms are ≥ 0 and,\allowbreak{} since 2t > 0,\allowbreak{} not both zero.\allowbreak{}\\
\ \ have hA : 0 ≤ (\allowbreak{}q - p) * (\allowbreak{}t + x) := Int.\allowbreak{}mul\_\allowbreak{}nonneg (\allowbreak{}by omega) (\allowbreak{}by omega)\\
\ \ have hB : 0 ≤ (\allowbreak{}q + p) * (\allowbreak{}t - x) := Int.\allowbreak{}mul\_\allowbreak{}nonneg (\allowbreak{}by omega) (\allowbreak{}by omega)\\
\ \ have h3 : 0 < (\allowbreak{}q - p) * (\allowbreak{}t + x) + (\allowbreak{}q + p) * (\allowbreak{}t - x) := by\\
\ \ \ \ by\_\allowbreak{}cases hx0 : 0 < t + x\\
\ \ \ \ · have : 0 < (\allowbreak{}q - p) * (\allowbreak{}t + x) := Int.\allowbreak{}mul\_\allowbreak{}pos (\allowbreak{}by omega) hx0\\
\ \ \ \ \ \ omega\\
\ \ \ \ · have : 0 < (\allowbreak{}q + p) * (\allowbreak{}t - x) := Int.\allowbreak{}mul\_\allowbreak{}pos (\allowbreak{}by omega) (\allowbreak{}by omega)\\
\ \ \ \ \ \ omega\\
\ \ unfold boostT; expand\_\allowbreak{}omega\end{lean}
It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{Quot.sound} (a quotient makes equal what its relation relates — the axiom behind function extensionality) and \texttt{propext} (two propositions that imply each other are the same proposition). \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Spacelike order reverses]
FOR A SPACELIKE SEPARATION THERE IS A FRAME BELOW c IN WHICH THE ORDER REVERSES — exhibited: with 0 < t < x, the boost β = (2t+1)/(2x) sends Δt to −x.

by\\
\ \ refine ⟨\allowbreak{}⟨\allowbreak{}by omega,\allowbreak{} by omega,\allowbreak{} by omega⟩,\allowbreak{} ?\_\allowbreak{}⟩\\
\ \ unfold boostT; expand\_\allowbreak{}omega\end{lean}

\begin{theorem}[Velocity addition below c]
TWO BOOSTS BELOW c COMPOSE TO A BOOST BELOW c, for every pair — c is not approached by adding.
\begin{lean}(p₁ q₁ p₂ q₂ : Int) (h₁ : belowC p₁ q₁) (h₂ : belowC p₂ q₂) : belowC (addNum p₁ q₁ p₂ q₂) (addDen p₁ q₁ p₂ q₂)\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{spacetime.lean}:\begin{lean}def belowC (\allowbreak{}p q : Int) : Prop := 0 < q ∧ -q < p ∧ p < q\\
\mbox{}\\
def addNum (\allowbreak{}p₁ q₁ p₂ q₂ : Int) : Int := p₁*q₂ + p₂*q₁\\
\mbox{}\\
def addDen (\allowbreak{}p₁ q₁ p₂ q₂ : Int) : Int := q₁*q₂ + p₁*p₂\end{lean}
The proof, verbatim as the Lean kernel checked it:\begin{lean}theorem velocity\_\allowbreak{}addition\_\allowbreak{}below\_\allowbreak{}c : (\allowbreak{}p₁ q₁ p₂ q₂ : Int) (\allowbreak{}h₁ : belowC p₁ q₁) (\allowbreak{}h₂ : belowC p₂ q₂) : belowC (\allowbreak{}addNum p₁ q₁ p₂ q₂) (\allowbreak{}addDen p₁ q₁ p₂ q₂) :=\\
by\\
\ \ obtain ⟨\allowbreak{}a,\allowbreak{} b,\allowbreak{} c⟩ := h₁; obtain ⟨\allowbreak{}d,\allowbreak{} e,\allowbreak{} f⟩ := h₂\\
\ \ -- den − num = (\allowbreak{}q₁−p₁)(\allowbreak{}q₂−p₂) and den + num = (\allowbreak{}q₁+p₁)(\allowbreak{}q₂+p₂): both positive,\allowbreak{} so |num| < den\\
\ \ have hm : 0 < (\allowbreak{}q₁ - p₁) * (\allowbreak{}q₂ - p₂) := Int.\allowbreak{}mul\_\allowbreak{}pos (\allowbreak{}by omega) (\allowbreak{}by omega)\\
\ \ have hp : 0 < (\allowbreak{}q₁ + p₁) * (\allowbreak{}q₂ + p₂) := Int.\allowbreak{}mul\_\allowbreak{}pos (\allowbreak{}by omega) (\allowbreak{}by omega)\\
\ \ have hq : 0 < q₁ * q₂ := Int.\allowbreak{}mul\_\allowbreak{}pos a d\\
\ \ unfold belowC addNum addDen\\
\ \ refine ⟨\allowbreak{}?\_\allowbreak{},\allowbreak{} ?\_\allowbreak{},\allowbreak{} ?\_\allowbreak{}⟩ <;> expand\_\allowbreak{}omega\end{lean}
It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{Quot.sound} (a quotient makes equal what its relation relates — the axiom behind function extensionality) and \texttt{propext} (two propositions that imply each other are the same proposition). \end{proof}
\subsection{\texttt{three.lean}}
\begin{theorem}[Closure is one hundred sixty two]
The closure has exactly rows x cols cells: 18 x 9 = 162 for the installed library.
\begin{lean}(cells 18 9).length = 162\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{three.lean}:\begin{lean}def cells (\allowbreak{}rows cols : Nat) : List (\allowbreak{}Nat × Nat) :=\\
\ \ (\allowbreak{}List.\allowbreak{}range rows).\allowbreak{}flatMap (\allowbreak{}fun g => (\allowbreak{}List.\allowbreak{}range cols).\allowbreak{}map (\allowbreak{}fun m => (\allowbreak{}g,\allowbreak{} m)))\end{lean}
The proof, verbatim as the Lean kernel checked it:\begin{lean}theorem closure\_\allowbreak{}is\_\allowbreak{}one\_\allowbreak{}hundred\_\allowbreak{}sixty\_\allowbreak{}two : (\allowbreak{}cells 1\allowbreak{}8 9).\allowbreak{}length = 1\allowbreak{}6\allowbreak{}2 := by decide\end{lean}
It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{of\_decide\_eq\_true} (the kernel itself: the statement reduces to true by computation, and the rule that turns that reduction into a proof rests on no axiom). \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Closure is the product]
The product law, at several shapes — the size is rows x cols and not an accident of 18 and 10.
\begin{lean}(cells 1 1).length = 1 ∧ (cells 8 8).length = 64 ∧ (cells 18 9).length = 162 ∧ (cells 9 18).length = 162 ∧ (cells 18 10).length = 180\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{three.lean}:\begin{lean}def cells (\allowbreak{}rows cols : Nat) : List (\allowbreak{}Nat × Nat) :=\\
\ \ (\allowbreak{}List.\allowbreak{}range rows).\allowbreak{}flatMap (\allowbreak{}fun g => (\allowbreak{}List.\allowbreak{}range cols).\allowbreak{}map (\allowbreak{}fun m => (\allowbreak{}g,\allowbreak{} m)))\end{lean}
The proof, verbatim as the Lean kernel checked it:\begin{lean}theorem closure\_\allowbreak{}is\_\allowbreak{}the\_\allowbreak{}product : (\allowbreak{}cells 1 1).\allowbreak{}length = 1 ∧ (\allowbreak{}cells 8 8).\allowbreak{}length = 6\allowbreak{}4 ∧ (\allowbreak{}cells 1\allowbreak{}8 9).\allowbreak{}length = 1\allowbreak{}6\allowbreak{}2 ∧ (\allowbreak{}cells 9 1\allowbreak{}8).\allowbreak{}length = 1\allowbreak{}6\allowbreak{}2 ∧ (\allowbreak{}cells 1\allowbreak{}8 1\allowbreak{}0).\allowbreak{}length = 1\allowbreak{}8\allowbreak{}0 := by decide\end{lean}
It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{of\_decide\_eq\_true} (the kernel itself: the statement reduces to true by computation, and the rule that turns that reduction into a proof rests on no axiom). \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Closure has no duplicate]
NO CELL IS REPEATED. This is the bijection, and it is strictly stronger than "every pair is present": a list carrying one pair twice and omitting another would satisfy presence at the right length, and would still have a hole in it.
\begin{lean}(cells 18 9).Nodup\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{three.lean}:\begin{lean}def cells (\allowbreak{}rows cols : Nat) : List (\allowbreak{}Nat × Nat) :=\\
\ \ (\allowbreak{}List.\allowbreak{}range rows).\allowbreak{}flatMap (\allowbreak{}fun g => (\allowbreak{}List.\allowbreak{}range cols).\allowbreak{}map (\allowbreak{}fun m => (\allowbreak{}g,\allowbreak{} m)))\end{lean}
The proof, verbatim as the Lean kernel checked it:\begin{lean}theorem closure\_\allowbreak{}has\_\allowbreak{}no\_\allowbreak{}duplicate : (\allowbreak{}cells 1\allowbreak{}8 9).\allowbreak{}Nodup := by decide\end{lean}
It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{of\_decide\_eq\_true} (the kernel itself: the statement reduces to true by computation, and the rule that turns that reduction into a proof rests on no axiom). \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Closure is complete]
\begin{lean}coversEveryPair 18 9 = true\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{three.lean}:\begin{lean}def cells (\allowbreak{}rows cols : Nat) : List (\allowbreak{}Nat × Nat) :=\\
\ \ (\allowbreak{}List.\allowbreak{}range rows).\allowbreak{}flatMap (\allowbreak{}fun g => (\allowbreak{}List.\allowbreak{}range cols).\allowbreak{}map (\allowbreak{}fun m => (\allowbreak{}g,\allowbreak{} m)))\\
\mbox{}\\
def coversEveryPair (\allowbreak{}rows cols : Nat) : Bool :=\\

\begin{theorem}[Reflection has no fixed point]
NO cell is its own reflection. ONE even side is enough: a fixed cell would need g = rows−1−g AND m = cols−1−m, so an even side makes its own coordinate unfixable and the conjunction fails whatever the other side does. The closure is 18 x 9 — the columns ARE odd, and m = 4 is fixed — yet no CELL is, because 18 is even. Both sides odd is the only case with a fixed point, exactly as the digit reflection d ↦ 10 − d fixes 5 and nothing else.

\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Chi and genus are inverse]
genus ∘ chi is the identity at every integer g: χ loses nothing about g.
\begin{lean}∀ g : Int, genus (chi g) = g\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright

by\\
\ \ intro g; unfold genus chi; omega\end{lean}
It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{Quot.sound} (a quotient makes equal what its relation relates — the axiom behind function extensionality) and \texttt{propext} (two propositions that imply each other are the same proposition). \end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Involution splits the middle forms]
The involution and the split it produces, for every 2-form v: v + ★v is self-dual, v − ★v is anti-self-dual, and the two halves add back to 2v. This is the F = F⁺ + F⁻ instantons are built on.

\begin{theorem}[Euler characteristic and genus are inverse]
χ and the genus are INVERSE: reading the genus back from χ(g) returns g for every surface up to genus 9, and rank H₁ = 2 − χ = 2g at each one. The corpus's own surface is the instance g = 2 — eulerChi is χ(2) and homologyLoops is 2 − χ(2) — derived by the law, not typed beside it.

\begin{theorem}[Odd cancels]
For any involution and any f, the odd part cancels over the orbit \{x, σ x\}.
\begin{lean}\{α : Type\} (f : α → Int) (σ : α → α) (h : IsInvolution σ) (x : α) : odd f σ x + odd f σ (σ x) = 0\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{cross.lean}:\begin{lean}def IsInvolution \{α : Type\} (\allowbreak{}σ : α → α) : Prop := ∀ x,\allowbreak{} σ (\allowbreak{}σ x) = x\\
\mbox{}\\
def odd \{α : Type\} (\allowbreak{}f : α → Int) (\allowbreak{}σ : α → α) (\allowbreak{}x : α) : Int := f x - f (\allowbreak{}σ x)\end{lean}
The proof, verbatim as the Lean kernel checked it:\begin{lean}theorem odd\_\allowbreak{}cancels : \{α : Type\} (\allowbreak{}f : α → Int) (\allowbreak{}σ : α → α) (\allowbreak{}h : IsInvolution σ) (\allowbreak{}x : α) : odd f σ x + odd f σ (\allowbreak{}σ x) = 0 :=\\
by\\
\ \ unfold odd\\
\ \ rw [\allowbreak{}h x]\\
\ \ omega\end{lean}
It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{Quot.sound} (a quotient makes equal what its relation relates — the axiom behind function extensionality) and \texttt{propext} (two propositions that imply each other are the same proposition). \end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[All holding is pleasant and calm]
All signals holding feels pleasant and calm.
\begin{lean}∀ n ∈ [0, 1, 2, 3, 6], feel (List.replicate n true) = pleasant ∧ arousal (List.replicate n true) = 0\end{lean}
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[H unitary]
HADAMARD IS UNITARY UP TO ITS RECORDED SCALE: H · H† = 2 · I.
\begin{lean}Same 2 (mm 2 H (dag H)) (smul 2 idm)\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{quantum.lean}:\begin{lean}structure GI where\\
\ \ re : Int\\
\ \ im : Int\\
\mbox{}\\
def sumTo (\allowbreak{}n : Nat) (\allowbreak{}f : Nat → GI) : GI := (\allowbreak{}List.\allowbreak{}range n).\allowbreak{}foldl (\allowbreak{}fun acc k => acc + f k) 0\\
\mbox{}\\
abbrev Mat := Nat → Nat → GI\\
\mbox{}\\
def mm (\allowbreak{}n : Nat) (\allowbreak{}a b : Mat) : Mat := fun r c => sumTo n fun k => a r k * b k c\\
\mbox{}\\
def dag (\allowbreak{}a : Mat) : Mat := fun r c => GI.\allowbreak{}conj (\allowbreak{}a c r)\\
\mbox{}\\
def idm : Mat := fun r c => if r = c then 1 else 0\\
\mbox{}\\
def smul (\allowbreak{}k : GI) (\allowbreak{}a : Mat) : Mat := fun r c => k * a r c\\
\mbox{}\\
def Same (\allowbreak{}n : Nat) (\allowbreak{}a b : Mat) : Prop := ∀ r,\allowbreak{} r < n → ∀ c,\allowbreak{} c < n → a r c = b r c\\
\mbox{}\\
def H : Mat := fun r c => if r = 1 ∧ c = 1 then -1 else 1\end{lean}

\begin{theorem}[Paulis unitary]
X, Z and S are unitary: U · U† = I.
\begin{lean}Same 2 (mm 2 X (dag X)) idm ∧ Same 2 (mm 2 Z (dag Z)) idm ∧ Same 2 (mm 2 S (dag S)) idm\end{lean}
\end{theorem}

\ \ im : Int\\

\mbox{}\\

\mbox{}\\

\mbox{}\\

\begin{theorem}[The two reflections connect the three trinities]

\begin{theorem}[A two to one fold of addresses is many to one by pigeonhole]

\begin{lean}eq (mul ⟨2,3⟩ ⟨5,7⟩) (mul ⟨5,7⟩ ⟨2,3⟩)\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright

\ \ num : Int\\
\ \ den : Int\\
\ \ deriving DecidableEq,\allowbreak{} Repr\\
\mbox{}\\
def eq (\allowbreak{}a b : Rat) : Prop := a.\allowbreak{}num * b.\allowbreak{}den = b.\allowbreak{}num * a.\allowbreak{}den\\
\mbox{}\\
def mul (\allowbreak{}a b : Rat) : Rat := ⟨\allowbreak{}a.\allowbreak{}num * b.\allowbreak{}num,\allowbreak{} a.\allowbreak{}den * b.\allowbreak{}den⟩\end{lean}
The proof, verbatim as the Lean kernel checked it:\begin{lean}theorem mul\_\allowbreak{}comm\_\allowbreak{}sample : eq (\allowbreak{}mul ⟨\allowbreak{}2,\allowbreak{}3⟩ ⟨\allowbreak{}5,\allowbreak{}7⟩) (\allowbreak{}mul ⟨\allowbreak{}5,\allowbreak{}7⟩ ⟨\allowbreak{}2,\allowbreak{}3⟩) := by decide\end{lean}
It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{of\_decide\_eq\_true} (the kernel itself: the statement reduces to true by computation, and the rule that turns that reduction into a proof rests on no axiom). \end{proof}

\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Graeco latin none of order two]
\begin{lean}order2.all (fun a => order2.all (fun b => !(latin 2 a \&\& latin 2 b \&\& orthogonal 2 a b))) = true\end{lean}
\end{theorem}

\ \ | [\allowbreak{}],\allowbreak{} \_\allowbreak{},\allowbreak{} d => d\\
\ \ | x :: \_\allowbreak{},\allowbreak{} 0,\allowbreak{} \_\allowbreak{} => x\\
\ \ | \_\allowbreak{} :: xs,\allowbreak{} k + 1,\allowbreak{} d => nth xs k d\\
\mbox{}\\
def row : List (\allowbreak{}List Nat) → Nat → List Nat\\
\ \ | [\allowbreak{}],\allowbreak{} \_\allowbreak{} => [\allowbreak{}]\\
\ \ | r :: \_\allowbreak{},\allowbreak{} 0 => r\\
\ \ | \_\allowbreak{} :: rs,\allowbreak{} k + 1 => row rs k\\
\mbox{}\\
def latin (\allowbreak{}n : Nat) (\allowbreak{}sq : List (\allowbreak{}List Nat)) : Bool :=\\
\ \ sq.\allowbreak{}length == n \&\& sq.\allowbreak{}all (\allowbreak{}fun r => r.\allowbreak{}length == n \&\& (\allowbreak{}List.\allowbreak{}range n).\allowbreak{}all (\allowbreak{}fun v => r.\allowbreak{}any (\allowbreak{}fun w => w == v))) \&\&\\

\mbox{}\\

\ \ let pairs := (\allowbreak{}List.\allowbreak{}range n).\allowbreak{}flatMap fun i => (\allowbreak{}List.\allowbreak{}range n).\allowbreak{}map fun j =>\\
\ \ \ \ (\allowbreak{}nth (\allowbreak{}row a i) j n,\allowbreak{} nth (\allowbreak{}row b i) j n)\\
\ \ (\allowbreak{}List.\allowbreak{}range n).\allowbreak{}all fun x => (\allowbreak{}List.\allowbreak{}range n).\allowbreak{}all fun y => pairs.\allowbreak{}any (\allowbreak{}fun q => q.\allowbreak{}1 == x \&\& q.\allowbreak{}2 == y)\\
\mbox{}\\
def order2 : List (\allowbreak{}List (\allowbreak{}List Nat)) := [\allowbreak{}[\allowbreak{}[\allowbreak{}0,\allowbreak{}1],\allowbreak{}[\allowbreak{}1,\allowbreak{}0]],\allowbreak{} [\allowbreak{}[\allowbreak{}1,\allowbreak{}0],\allowbreak{}[\allowbreak{}0,\allowbreak{}1]]]\end{lean}

\begin{theorem}[Kummer instances]
\begin{lean}[2, 3, 5].all (fun p => (List.range 12).all (fun m => (List.range 12).all (fun n => vp p 64 (choose' (m + n) n) == carries p 16 m n 0))) = true\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{registry.lean}:\begin{lean}def fact : Nat → Nat | 0 => 1 | k + 1 => (\allowbreak{}k + 1) * fact k\\
\mbox{}\\
def choose' (\allowbreak{}a b : Nat) : Nat := fact a / (\allowbreak{}fact b * fact (\allowbreak{}a - b))\\
\mbox{}\\
def vp (\allowbreak{}p : Nat) : Nat → Nat → Nat\\
\ \ | 0,\allowbreak{} \_\allowbreak{} => 0\\

\begin{theorem}[Circle of fifths does not close]
The circle of fifths does not close: twelve perfect fifths overshoot seven octaves by the Pythagorean comma, (3/2)¹² / 2⁷ = 3¹² / 2¹⁹ = 531441 / 524288. Cross-multiplied, so no division enters; 3¹² sits strictly between 2¹⁹ and 2²⁰, so no number of octaves meets it.

\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[The sigma trapdoor is fermats difference of squares]
\begin{lean}oddPrimes = [3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23, 29] ∧ oddPrimes.all (fun p => oddPrimes.all (fun q => !(p < q) || witness p q * witness p q - p * q == ((q - p) / 2) * ((q - p) / 2))) ∧ oddPrimes.all (fun p => oddPrimes.all (fun q => !(p < q) || splits (p * q) == [(p, q)])) ∧ oddPrimes.all (fun p => oddPrimes.all (fun q => !(p < q) || decodes (p * q) (witness p q))) ∧ oddPrimes.all (fun q => (2 + q) \% 2 == 1)\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{thousand.lean}:\begin{lean}def isPrime (\allowbreak{}n : Nat) : Bool := n ≥ 2 \&\& (\allowbreak{}List.\allowbreak{}range' 2 (\allowbreak{}n - 2)).\allowbreak{}all (\allowbreak{}fun d => n \% d != 0)\\
\mbox{}\\
def oddPrimes : List Nat := (\allowbreak{}List.\allowbreak{}range' 3 2\allowbreak{}7).\allowbreak{}filter isPrime\\
\mbox{}\\
def splits (\allowbreak{}N : Nat) : List (\allowbreak{}Nat × Nat) := (\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{}List.\allowbreak{}range' 2 N).\allowbreak{}filter (\allowbreak{}fun u => N \% u == 0 \&\& u * u ≤ N)).\allowbreak{}map (\allowbreak{}fun u => (\allowbreak{}u,\allowbreak{} N / u))\\
\mbox{}\\
def witness (\allowbreak{}p q : Nat) : Nat := (\allowbreak{}p + q) / 2\\
\mbox{}\\
def decodes (\allowbreak{}N x : Nat) : Bool := (\allowbreak{}List.\allowbreak{}range' 0 (\allowbreak{}x - 1)).\allowbreak{}any (\allowbreak{}fun b => (\allowbreak{}x - b) * (\allowbreak{}x + b) == N)\end{lean}

It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{of\_decide\_eq\_true} (the kernel itself: the statement reduces to true by computation, and the rule that turns that reduction into a proof rests on no axiom). \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[A wrong witness decodes nothing because a semiprime has one split]
\begin{lean}small = [3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19] ∧ small.all (fun p => small.all (fun q => !(p < q) || (List.range' (ceilSqrt (p * q)) ((p * q + 1) / 2 - ceilSqrt (p * q))).all (fun x => decodes (p * q) x == (x == witness p q))))\end{lean}

\begin{theorem}[An impossible integer with twin primes is opened blind in one reflection]
\begin{lean}blind 11 13 = 1 ∧ blind 5 7 = 1 ∧ blind 3 29 = 7 ∧ (oddPrimes.filter (fun p => isPrime (p + 2))) = [3, 5, 11, 17, 29] ∧ oddPrimes.all (fun p => !(isPrime (p + 2)) || blind p (p + 2) == 1) ∧ oddPrimes.all (fun p => oddPrimes.all (fun q => !(p < q) || blind p q ≥ 1)) ∧ blind 3 29 > blind 3 5\end{lean}
\end{theorem}

\mbox{}\\
def oddPrimes : List Nat := (\allowbreak{}List.\allowbreak{}range' 3 2\allowbreak{}7).\allowbreak{}filter isPrime\\
\mbox{}\\
def ceilSqrt (\allowbreak{}N : Nat) : Nat := (\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{}List.\allowbreak{}range' 0 (\allowbreak{}N + 1)).\allowbreak{}find? (\allowbreak{}fun x => x * x ≥ N)).\allowbreak{}getD 0\\
\mbox{}\\
def witness (\allowbreak{}p q : Nat) : Nat := (\allowbreak{}p + q) / 2\\

def blind (\allowbreak{}p q : Nat) : Nat := witness p q - ceilSqrt (\allowbreak{}p * q) + 1\end{lean}

\begin{theorem}[The descent is strictly monotone]
THE RATCHET LAW over the real history, read newest-first: each count is strictly below the one before it. A wave that added an index.ts would make this proof fail, which is exactly what "the count may fall, never rise" means when it is checkable.  The pairs are DERIVED from `recorded` — `recorded.zip recorded.tail` is the consecutive pairing — because they used to be typed out a second time and that second copy rotted: the corpus descended to 138, the record above followed, and this list did not. It went on proving a true fact about a history that had stopped being the whole history, which is the exact failure the comment on `recorded` describes, committed one definition further down. A record read twice is a record that can disagree with itself.
\begin{lean}(∀ p ∈ recorded.zip recorded.tail, p.1 < p.2)\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright

The proof, verbatim as the Lean kernel checked it:\begin{lean}theorem the\_\allowbreak{}descent\_\allowbreak{}is\_\allowbreak{}strictly\_\allowbreak{}monotone : (\allowbreak{}∀ p ∈ recorded.\allowbreak{}zip recorded.\allowbreak{}tail,\allowbreak{} p.\allowbreak{}1 < p.\allowbreak{}2) := by decide\end{lean}

\begin{theorem}[Poincare is an inverse pair and reflects to the frontier]
genus ∘ chi is the identity at every integer, chi ∘ chi is not, and σ carries the station to 9 (a digit of the walk; the smooth four-dimensional Poincaré question is open, and nothing here bears on it).
\begin{lean}(∀ g : Int, genus (chi g) = g) ∧ chi (chi 0) ≠ 0 ∧ reflect 1 = 9\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{one.lean}:\begin{lean}def reflect (\allowbreak{}d : Nat) : Nat := (\allowbreak{}1\allowbreak{}0 - d) \% 1\allowbreak{}0\\
\mbox{}\\
def chi (\allowbreak{}g : Int) : Int := 2 - 2 * g\\
\mbox{}\\
def genus (\allowbreak{}c : Int) : Int := (\allowbreak{}2 - c) / 2\end{lean}

by\\
\ \ refine ⟨\allowbreak{}fun g => ?\_\allowbreak{},\allowbreak{} by decide,\allowbreak{} by decide⟩\\
\ \ unfold genus chi; omega\end{lean}
It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{Quot.sound} (a quotient makes equal what its relation relates — the axiom behind function extensionality) and \texttt{propext} (two propositions that imply each other are the same proposition). \end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[From two the sequence is one cycle through every station]
From 2 the walk is one cycle through all ten stations, home after exactly ten steps and never sooner.
\begin{lean}(∀ e : Fin 10, walk 2 (stepsTo 2 e.val) = e.val) ∧ walk 2 10 = 2 ∧ (∀ k : Fin 10, k.val ≠ 0 → walk 2 k.val ≠ 2)\end{lean}

\begin{theorem}[Walking from the mirror is walking from here shifted]

\subsection{\texttt{four.lean}}
\begin{theorem}[From four the sequence is one cycle through every station]
From 4 the walk is one cycle through all ten stations, home after exactly ten steps and never sooner.
\begin{lean}(∀ e : Fin 10, walk 4 (stepsTo 4 e.val) = e.val) ∧ walk 4 10 = 4 ∧ (∀ k : Fin 10, k.val ≠ 0 → walk 4 k.val ≠ 4)\end{lean}
\end{theorem}

\mbox{}\\

\mbox{}\\

\ \ | 1 => 0 | 2 => 1 | 4 => 2 | 8 => 3 | 7 => 4 | 5 => 5 | 3 => 6 | 6 => 7 | 9 => 8 | 0 => 9 | \_\allowbreak{} => 0\\

\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[At four the reflection lags the walk by one step]

\begin{lean}(10 - 2 * 4 \% 9) \% 9 = (2 * ((10 - 4) \% 9) + 8) \% 9 ∧ (10 - 2 * 4 \% 9) \% 9 ≠ 2 * ((10 - 4) \% 9) \% 9\end{lean}

\begin{theorem}[From four walking the reflection experiences the sequence]
From 4, walking the reflection IS experiencing the sequence from 6, seen through σ — one cycle through every station.
\begin{lean}(∀ k : Fin 10, mirrorWalk 4 k.val = reflect (walk 6 k.val)) ∧ (∀ e : Fin 10, mirrorWalk 4 (stepsTo 6 (reflect e.val)) = e.val) ∧ mirrorWalk 4 10 = 4\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{four.lean}:\begin{lean}def next : Nat → Nat\\
\ \ | 1 => 2 | 2 => 4 | 4 => 8 | 8 => 7 | 7 => 5 | 5 => 3 | 3 => 6 | 6 => 9 | 9 => 0 | 0 => 1 | n => n\\
\mbox{}\\
def walk (\allowbreak{}d k : Nat) : Nat := Nat.\allowbreak{}repeat next k d\\
\mbox{}\\
def pos : Nat → Nat\\
\ \ | 1 => 0 | 2 => 1 | 4 => 2 | 8 => 3 | 7 => 4 | 5 => 5 | 3 => 6 | 6 => 7 | 9 => 8 | 0 => 9 | \_\allowbreak{} => 0\\
\mbox{}\\
def stepsTo (\allowbreak{}d e : Nat) : Nat := (\allowbreak{}pos e + 1\allowbreak{}0 - pos d) \% 1\allowbreak{}0\\
\mbox{}\\
def reflect (\allowbreak{}d : Nat) : Nat := (\allowbreak{}1\allowbreak{}0 - d) \% 1\allowbreak{}0\\
\mbox{}\\
def mirrorNext (\allowbreak{}d : Nat) : Nat := reflect (\allowbreak{}next (\allowbreak{}reflect d))\\

\begin{theorem}[Compl compl]
Complementing a language twice returns it — canonical in p-vs-np.lean.
\begin{lean}∀ L : Lang, compl (compl L) = L\end{lean}

by\\
\ \ intro L; funext w; simp [\allowbreak{}compl]\end{lean}
It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{Quot.sound} (a quotient makes equal what its relation relates — the axiom behind function extensionality) and \texttt{propext} (two propositions that imply each other are the same proposition). \end{proof}

\subsection{\texttt{five.lean}}
\begin{theorem}[The sequence is one cycle through every station]
The walk is ONE cycle through all ten stations: from every station it reaches every station, and returns after exactly ten steps, never sooner.
\begin{lean}(∀ d e : Fin 10, walk d.val (stepsTo d.val e.val) = e.val) ∧ (∀ d : Fin 10, walk d.val 10 = d.val) ∧ (∀ d k : Fin 10, k.val ≠ 0 → walk d.val k.val ≠ d.val)\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{five.lean}:\begin{lean}def next : Nat → Nat\\
\ \ | 1 => 2 | 2 => 4 | 4 => 8 | 8 => 7 | 7 => 5 | 5 => 3 | 3 => 6 | 6 => 9 | 9 => 0 | 0 => 1 | n => n\\
\mbox{}\\
def walk (\allowbreak{}d k : Nat) : Nat := Nat.\allowbreak{}repeat next k d\\
\mbox{}\\
def pos : Nat → Nat\\
\ \ | 1 => 0 | 2 => 1 | 4 => 2 | 8 => 3 | 7 => 4 | 5 => 5 | 3 => 6 | 6 => 7 | 9 => 8 | 0 => 9 | \_\allowbreak{} => 0\\
\mbox{}\\
def stepsTo (\allowbreak{}d e : Nat) : Nat := (\allowbreak{}pos e + 1\allowbreak{}0 - pos d) \% 1\allowbreak{}0\end{lean}
The proof, verbatim as the Lean kernel checked it:\begin{lean}theorem the\_\allowbreak{}sequence\_\allowbreak{}is\_\allowbreak{}one\_\allowbreak{}cycle\_\allowbreak{}through\_\allowbreak{}every\_\allowbreak{}station : (\allowbreak{}∀ d e : Fin 1\allowbreak{}0,\allowbreak{} walk d.\allowbreak{}val (\allowbreak{}stepsTo d.\allowbreak{}val e.\allowbreak{}val) = e.\allowbreak{}val) ∧ (\allowbreak{}∀ d : Fin 1\allowbreak{}0,\allowbreak{} walk d.\allowbreak{}val 1\allowbreak{}0 = d.\allowbreak{}val) ∧ (\allowbreak{}∀ d k : Fin 1\allowbreak{}0,\allowbreak{} k.\allowbreak{}val ≠ 0 → walk d.\allowbreak{}val k.\allowbreak{}val ≠ d.\allowbreak{}val) := by decide\end{lean}
It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{of\_decide\_eq\_true} (the kernel itself: the statement reduces to true by computation, and the rule that turns that reduction into a proof rests on no axiom). \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Forward doubles and five undoes it]
Forward is ×2 mod 9 on the doubling orbit, and ×5 undoes it; the four remaining steps leave the doubling.
\begin{lean}(∀ d ∈ [1, 2, 4, 8, 7], next d = 2 * d \% 9 ∧ 5 * next d \% 9 = d) ∧ next 5 = 3 ∧ 2 * 5 \% 9 ≠ 3 ∧ next 3 = 6 ∧ next 6 = 9 ∧ next 9 = 0 ∧ next 0 = 1\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{five.lean}:\begin{lean}def next : Nat → Nat\\
\ \ | 1 => 2 | 2 => 4 | 4 => 8 | 8 => 7 | 7 => 5 | 5 => 3 | 3 => 6 | 6 => 9 | 9 => 0 | 0 => 1 | n => n\end{lean}
The proof, verbatim as the Lean kernel checked it:\begin{lean}theorem forward\_\allowbreak{}doubles\_\allowbreak{}and\_\allowbreak{}five\_\allowbreak{}undoes\_\allowbreak{}it : (\allowbreak{}∀ d ∈ [\allowbreak{}1,\allowbreak{} 2,\allowbreak{} 4,\allowbreak{} 8,\allowbreak{} 7],\allowbreak{} next d = 2 * d \% 9 ∧ 5 * next d \% 9 = d) ∧ next 5 = 3 ∧ 2 * 5 \% 9 ≠ 3 ∧ next 3 = 6 ∧ next 6 = 9 ∧ next 9 = 0 ∧ next 0 = 1 := by decide\end{lean}
It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{of\_decide\_eq\_true} (the kernel itself: the statement reduces to true by computation, and the rule that turns that reduction into a proof rests on no axiom). \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Reflect is an involution fixing zero and five]
σ is an involution on the ten stations, fixing exactly the void 0 and the centre 5.
\begin{lean}(∀ d : Fin 10, reflect (reflect d.val) = d.val) ∧ (List.range 10).filter (fun d => reflect d == d) = [0, 5]\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{five.lean}:\begin{lean}def reflect (\allowbreak{}d : Nat) : Nat := (\allowbreak{}1\allowbreak{}0 - d) \% 1\allowbreak{}0\end{lean}
The proof, verbatim as the Lean kernel checked it:\begin{lean}theorem reflect\_\allowbreak{}is\_\allowbreak{}an\_\allowbreak{}involution\_\allowbreak{}fixing\_\allowbreak{}zero\_\allowbreak{}and\_\allowbreak{}five : (\allowbreak{}∀ d : Fin 1\allowbreak{}0,\allowbreak{} reflect (\allowbreak{}reflect d.\allowbreak{}val) = d.\allowbreak{}val) ∧ (\allowbreak{}List.\allowbreak{}range 1\allowbreak{}0).\allowbreak{}filter (\allowbreak{}fun d => reflect d == d) = [\allowbreak{}0,\allowbreak{} 5] := by decide\end{lean}
It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{of\_decide\_eq\_true} (the kernel itself: the statement reduces to true by computation, and the rule that turns that reduction into a proof rests on no axiom). \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Reflection lags the walk by one step]
σ does NOT commute with the walk: mod 9, reflecting then doubling is always one step behind doubling the reflection — σ(2d) ≡ 2σ(d) − 1 — never equal to it.
\begin{lean}∀ d : Fin 9, (10 - 2 * d.val \% 9) \% 9 = (2 * ((10 - d.val) \% 9) + 8) \% 9 ∧ (10 - 2 * d.val \% 9) \% 9 ≠ 2 * ((10 - d.val) \% 9) \% 9\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright

It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{of\_decide\_eq\_true} (the kernel itself: the statement reduces to true by computation, and the rule that turns that reduction into a proof rests on no axiom). \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Nine complement commutes with the walk]
The nine-complement d ↦ 9 − d DOES commute with the walk — the other involution, centred at 0.
\begin{lean}∀ d : Fin 9, (9 - 2 * d.val \% 9) \% 9 = 2 * ((9 - d.val) \% 9) \% 9\end{lean}
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Prev undoes next]
\begin{lean}∀ d : Fin 10, prev (next d.val) = d.val ∧ next (prev d.val) = d.val\end{lean}
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Walking the reflection experiences the sequence]
Walking the reflection IS experiencing the sequence: every step of the mirror walk from d is σ of the sequence's step from σ(d) — and it is one cycle through all ten stations, returning after exactly ten.
\begin{lean}(∀ d k : Fin 10, mirrorWalk d.val k.val = reflect (walk (reflect d.val) k.val)) ∧ (∀ d e : Fin 10, mirrorWalk d.val (stepsTo (reflect d.val) (reflect e.val)) = e.val) ∧ (∀ d : Fin 10, mirrorWalk d.val 10 = d.val) ∧ (∀ d k : Fin 10, k.val ≠ 0 → mirrorWalk d.val k.val ≠ d.val)\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright
Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{five.lean}:\begin{lean}def next : Nat → Nat\\
\ \ | 1 => 2 | 2 => 4 | 4 => 8 | 8 => 7 | 7 => 5 | 5 => 3 | 3 => 6 | 6 => 9 | 9 => 0 | 0 => 1 | n => n\\
\mbox{}\\
def walk (\allowbreak{}d k : Nat) : Nat := Nat.\allowbreak{}repeat next k d\\
\mbox{}\\
def pos : Nat → Nat\\
\ \ | 1 => 0 | 2 => 1 | 4 => 2 | 8 => 3 | 7 => 4 | 5 => 5 | 3 => 6 | 6 => 7 | 9 => 8 | 0 => 9 | \_\allowbreak{} => 0\\
\mbox{}\\
def stepsTo (\allowbreak{}d e : Nat) : Nat := (\allowbreak{}pos e + 1\allowbreak{}0 - pos d) \% 1\allowbreak{}0\\
\mbox{}\\
def reflect (\allowbreak{}d : Nat) : Nat := (\allowbreak{}1\allowbreak{}0 - d) \% 1\allowbreak{}0\\
\mbox{}\\
def mirrorNext (\allowbreak{}d : Nat) : Nat := reflect (\allowbreak{}next (\allowbreak{}reflect d))\\
\mbox{}\\
def mirrorWalk (\allowbreak{}d k : Nat) : Nat := Nat.\allowbreak{}repeat mirrorNext k d\end{lean}

Mirroring the mirror walk is the sequence again: σ applied twice changes nothing.

\begin{theorem}[The four faces are distinct]
THE FOUR FACES ARE DISTINCT: the sequence, its backward walk, the reflection walk and its backward walk are four different maps on the ten stations — because σ does not commute with the walk, the mirror is not the sequence and not its reverse.

\ \ \ \ face next ≠ face prev ∧ face next ≠ face mirrorNext ∧ face next ≠ face mirrorPrev ∧\\
\ \ \ \ face prev ≠ face mirrorNext ∧ face prev ≠ face mirrorPrev ∧ face mirrorNext ≠ face mirrorPrev := by decide\end{lean}

\begin{theorem}[From six the sequence is one cycle through every station]
From 6 the walk is one cycle through all ten stations, home after exactly ten steps and never sooner.
\begin{lean}(∀ e : Fin 10, walk 6 (stepsTo 6 e.val) = e.val) ∧ walk 6 10 = 6 ∧ (∀ k : Fin 10, k.val ≠ 0 → walk 6 k.val ≠ 6)\end{lean}
\end{theorem}

Definitions it unfolds, from \texttt{six.lean}:\begin{lean}def next : Nat → Nat\\
\ \ | 1 => 2 | 2 => 4 | 4 => 8 | 8 => 7 | 7 => 5 | 5 => 3 | 3 => 6 | 6 => 9 | 9 => 0 | 0 => 1 | n => n\\
\mbox{}\\
def walk (\allowbreak{}d k : Nat) : Nat := Nat.\allowbreak{}repeat next k d\\
\mbox{}\\
def pos : Nat → Nat\\
\ \ | 1 => 0 | 2 => 1 | 4 => 2 | 8 => 3 | 7 => 4 | 5 => 5 | 3 => 6 | 6 => 7 | 9 => 8 | 0 => 9 | \_\allowbreak{} => 0\\
\mbox{}\\
def stepsTo (\allowbreak{}d e : Nat) : Nat := (\allowbreak{}pos e + 1\allowbreak{}0 - pos d) \% 1\allowbreak{}0\end{lean}

It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{of\_decide\_eq\_true} (the kernel itself: the statement reduces to true by computation, and the rule that turns that reduction into a proof rests on no axiom). \end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[From six walking the reflection experiences the sequence]
From 6, walking the reflection IS experiencing the sequence from 4, seen through σ — one cycle through every station.
\begin{lean}(∀ k : Fin 10, mirrorWalk 6 k.val = reflect (walk 4 k.val)) ∧ (∀ e : Fin 10, mirrorWalk 6 (stepsTo 4 (reflect e.val)) = e.val) ∧ mirrorWalk 6 10 = 6\end{lean}
\end{theorem}

\mbox{}\\

\begin{lean}(∀ e : Fin 10, walk 8 (stepsTo 8 e.val) = e.val) ∧ walk 8 10 = 8 ∧ (∀ k : Fin 10, k.val ≠ 0 → walk 8 k.val ≠ 8)\end{lean}

\begin{theorem}[Star is an involution and reflects to riemann]
The star squares to the identity, and σ carries the station to Riemann's 2.
\begin{lean}(∀ v : Form2, star (star v) = v) ∧ reflect 8 = 2\end{lean}
\end{theorem}

structure Form2 where\\
\ \ e1\allowbreak{}2 : Int\\
\ \ e1\allowbreak{}3 : Int\\
\ \ e1\allowbreak{}4 : Int\\
\ \ e2\allowbreak{}3 : Int\\
\ \ e2\allowbreak{}4 : Int\\
\ \ e3\allowbreak{}4 : Int\\
\ \ deriving DecidableEq,\allowbreak{} Repr\\
\mbox{}\\
def star (\allowbreak{}v : Form2) : Form2 := ⟨\allowbreak{}v.\allowbreak{}e3\allowbreak{}4,\allowbreak{} -v.\allowbreak{}e2\allowbreak{}4,\allowbreak{} v.\allowbreak{}e2\allowbreak{}3,\allowbreak{} v.\allowbreak{}e1\allowbreak{}4,\allowbreak{} -v.\allowbreak{}e1\allowbreak{}3,\allowbreak{} v.\allowbreak{}e1\allowbreak{}2⟩\end{lean}

by\\
\ \ refine ⟨\allowbreak{}fun v => ?\_\allowbreak{},\allowbreak{} by decide⟩\\
\ \ cases v; simp only [\allowbreak{}star,\allowbreak{} Int.\allowbreak{}neg\_\allowbreak{}neg]\end{lean}
It rests on: debit: this theorem; credit: \texttt{propext} (two propositions that imply each other are the same proposition). \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Star negates every anti self dual form]

\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright

\ \ e1\allowbreak{}2 : Int\\
\ \ e1\allowbreak{}3 : Int\\

\ \ deriving DecidableEq,\allowbreak{} Repr\\
\mbox{}\\
def star (\allowbreak{}v : Form2) : Form2 := ⟨\allowbreak{}v.\allowbreak{}e3\allowbreak{}4,\allowbreak{} -v.\allowbreak{}e2\allowbreak{}4,\allowbreak{} v.\allowbreak{}e2\allowbreak{}3,\allowbreak{} v.\allowbreak{}e1\allowbreak{}4,\allowbreak{} -v.\allowbreak{}e1\allowbreak{}3,\allowbreak{} v.\allowbreak{}e1\allowbreak{}2⟩\\
\mbox{}\\
def neg (\allowbreak{}v : Form2) : Form2 := ⟨\allowbreak{}-v.\allowbreak{}e1\allowbreak{}2,\allowbreak{} -v.\allowbreak{}e1\allowbreak{}3,\allowbreak{} -v.\allowbreak{}e1\allowbreak{}4,\allowbreak{} -v.\allowbreak{}e2\allowbreak{}3,\allowbreak{} -v.\allowbreak{}e2\allowbreak{}4,\allowbreak{} -v.\allowbreak{}e3\allowbreak{}4⟩\\
\mbox{}\\
def asd (\allowbreak{}v : Form2) : Form2 :=\\
\ \ ⟨\allowbreak{}v.\allowbreak{}e1\allowbreak{}2 - v.\allowbreak{}e3\allowbreak{}4,\allowbreak{} v.\allowbreak{}e1\allowbreak{}3 + v.\allowbreak{}e2\allowbreak{}4,\allowbreak{} v.\allowbreak{}e1\allowbreak{}4 - v.\allowbreak{}e2\allowbreak{}3,\allowbreak{} v.\allowbreak{}e2\allowbreak{}3 - v.\allowbreak{}e1\allowbreak{}4,\allowbreak{} v.\allowbreak{}e2\allowbreak{}4 + v.\allowbreak{}e1\allowbreak{}3,\allowbreak{} v.\allowbreak{}e3\allowbreak{}4 - v.\allowbreak{}e1\allowbreak{}2⟩\end{lean}

by\\

\subsection{\texttt{nine.lean}}
\begin{theorem}[From nine the sequence is one cycle through every station]
From 9 the walk is one cycle through all ten stations, home after exactly ten steps and never sooner.
\begin{lean}(∀ e : Fin 10, walk 9 (stepsTo 9 e.val) = e.val) ∧ walk 9 10 = 9 ∧ (∀ k : Fin 10, k.val ≠ 0 → walk 9 k.val ≠ 9)\end{lean}
\end{theorem}

\ \ | 1 => 2 | 2 => 4 | 4 => 8 | 8 => 7 | 7 => 5 | 5 => 3 | 3 => 6 | 6 => 9 | 9 => 0 | 0 => 1 | n => n\\
\mbox{}\\
def walk (\allowbreak{}d k : Nat) : Nat := Nat.\allowbreak{}repeat next k d\\
\mbox{}\\
def pos : Nat → Nat\\
\ \ | 1 => 0 | 2 => 1 | 4 => 2 | 8 => 3 | 7 => 4 | 5 => 5 | 3 => 6 | 6 => 7 | 9 => 8 | 0 => 9 | \_\allowbreak{} => 0\\
\mbox{}\\
def stepsTo (\allowbreak{}d e : Nat) : Nat := (\allowbreak{}pos e + 1\allowbreak{}0 - pos d) \% 1\allowbreak{}0\end{lean}

\begin{theorem}[The step out of nine]
The step out of 9 goes to 0, which IS doubling mod 9.
\begin{lean}next 9 = 0 ∧ 2 * 9 \% 9 = 0 \% 9\end{lean}
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[At nine the reflection lags the walk by one step]
At 9, reflecting then doubling is one step behind doubling the reflection, mod 9 — never equal.
\begin{lean}(10 - 2 * 9 \% 9) \% 9 = (2 * ((10 - 9) \% 9) + 8) \% 9 ∧ (10 - 2 * 9 \% 9) \% 9 ≠ 2 * ((10 - 9) \% 9) \% 9\end{lean}

\begin{theorem}[From nine walking the reflection experiences the sequence]
From 9, walking the reflection IS experiencing the sequence from 1, seen through σ — one cycle through every station.
\begin{lean}(∀ k : Fin 10, mirrorWalk 9 k.val = reflect (walk 1 k.val)) ∧ (∀ e : Fin 10, mirrorWalk 9 (stepsTo 1 (reflect e.val)) = e.val) ∧ mirrorWalk 9 10 = 9\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright

\mbox{}\\
def walk (\allowbreak{}d k : Nat) : Nat := Nat.\allowbreak{}repeat next k d\\

def pos : Nat → Nat\\
\ \ | 1 => 0 | 2 => 1 | 4 => 2 | 8 => 3 | 7 => 4 | 5 => 5 | 3 => 6 | 6 => 7 | 9 => 8 | 0 => 9 | \_\allowbreak{} => 0\\
\mbox{}\\
def stepsTo (\allowbreak{}d e : Nat) : Nat := (\allowbreak{}pos e + 1\allowbreak{}0 - pos d) \% 1\allowbreak{}0\\
\mbox{}\\
def reflect (\allowbreak{}d : Nat) : Nat := (\allowbreak{}1\allowbreak{}0 - d) \% 1\allowbreak{}0\\
\mbox{}\\
def mirrorNext (\allowbreak{}d : Nat) : Nat := reflect (\allowbreak{}next (\allowbreak{}reflect d))\\
